chapters.title: Chapter 3: How Property Makes and Loses Money

lessons.title: Home Loans and Leverage: How EMIs Change Your Real Return

children.text: Every home loan sanction letter shows two numbers everyone reads: the loan amount and the EMI. For an ₹80 lakh loan at 8% over 20 years, that is ₹80 lakh and ₹66,915 a month. There is a third number almost nobody calculates: the total interest. On that loan, it is ₹80.6 lakh, more than the amount borrowed. A home loan is the most powerful tool in Indian real estate, and the most misunderstood. This lesson shows you exactly when it makes you richer and when it quietly does the opposite.

body.text: A home loan is leverage. It raises your return only when the property earns more than the loan costs. When it earns less, the loan makes you poorer while making you feel richer.

children.text: How an EMI Is Calculated

markDefs.definition: Equated Monthly Instalment: a fixed monthly payment that covers both interest and repayment of principal, calculated so the loan is fully repaid by the end of its tenure.

children.text: An
EMI

stays the same each month, as long as the interest rate does not change, but what it pays for shifts over time. Every month, interest is charged on the outstanding balance, and whatever is left of the EMI reduces the principal.

body.caption: P is the loan amount, r is the monthly interest rate (annual rate ÷ 12), and n is the number of monthly instalments.

body.label: ₹80 lakh loan at 8% for 20 years
body.context: Over 240 months you pay ₹1.61 crore in total: ₹80 lakh of principal and ₹80.6 lakh of interest. The interest alone costs more than the loan.

body.title: Calculate an EMI
body.prompt: Using the formula or the calculator above, what is the monthly EMI on a ₹50 lakh home loan at 8.5% a year for 20 years, in ₹? Round to the nearest rupee.
body.explanation: r = 8.5% ÷ 12 = 0.7083% a month, n = 240. EMI = ₹50,00,000 × r(1+r)^240 ÷ ((1+r)^240 minus 1) ≈ ₹43,391. Over 20 years you would pay about ₹1.04 crore in total, of which about ₹54 lakh is interest.

children.text: Early EMIs Are Mostly Interest

markDefs.definition: The schedule showing how each EMI is split between interest and principal, and how the outstanding loan balance falls over time.

children.text: Because interest is charged on the outstanding balance, and the balance is highest at the start, the first years of EMIs go mostly to the bank. Your lender's
amortisation schedule
shows this clearly. For the ₹80 lakh loan, ₹53,333 of the very first ₹66,915 EMI is interest.

body.title: Where each year's EMIs go: ₹80 lakh loan at 8% for 20 years (₹ lakh)

body.caption: How much you still owe on the ₹80 lakh loan

body.text: After 10 years and ₹80.3 lakh of EMIs, you still owe ₹55.15 lakh on an ₹80 lakh loan. Interest does not overtake principal repayment until year 12. This is why selling a flat a few years after buying it often returns far less cash than people expect: most of what they paid went to interest, not ownership.

body.title: Interest in your first EMI
body.prompt: On a ₹50 lakh home loan at 8.5% a year, how much of the very first monthly EMI is interest, in ₹? Round to the nearest rupee.
body.explanation: First month's interest = ₹50,00,000 × 8.5% ÷ 12 = ₹35,417. Of the ₹43,391 EMI, only about ₹7,974 reduces the principal in month one.

children.text: How Much Will a Bank Lend You?

markDefs.definition: Loan-to-Value ratio: the loan amount as a percentage of the property's value. RBI caps it based on loan size.

children.text: Two limits decide your loan. The first is the RBI's cap on the
LTV ratio

. The second is your income: lenders typically want your total EMIs, including car and personal loans, to stay within roughly 40% to 50% of your monthly take-home income, though exact limits vary by lender.

body.caption: RBI loan-to-value caps on home loans

body.title: Name the ratio
body.textWithBlank: The loan amount expressed as a percentage of the property's value is called the loan-to-___ ratio.
body.explanation: Loan-to-value, or LTV. For a ₹1.2 crore flat, a loan above ₹75 lakh is capped at 75% LTV, so the buyer must fund at least ₹30 lakh, plus stamp duty and other costs, from savings.

children.text: Floating Rates: When the RBI Moves, Your Loan Moves

markDefs.definition: External Benchmark Lending Rate: a bank's lending rate linked to an external benchmark, usually the RBI repo rate, plus a spread. When the benchmark changes, loans linked to it are reset.

children.text: Most Indian home loans are floating-rate loans linked to an
external benchmark

, usually the RBI repo rate. When the RBI raises or cuts the repo rate, your loan rate follows at the next reset. Between May 2022 and February 2023, the RBI raised the repo rate by 2.5 percentage points, and millions of borrowers saw their loans stretch out by years.

body.caption: What a 1 percentage point rate rise does to an ₹80 lakh, 20-year loan

cells: Rate rises to 9%, tenure extended instead

body.text: When rates rise, many lenders keep your EMI unchanged and quietly extend the tenure. It feels painless, but in our example a 1 point rise added more than five years of payments and about ₹42 lakh of extra interest. When your loan rate changes, ask your lender for the revised schedule and consider raising the EMI instead.

children.text: Prepayment: The Cheapest Return You Can Earn
Every extra rupee you pay towards principal saves interest at your loan rate, guaranteed. Paying just ₹10,000 a month above the ₹66,915 EMI on our ₹80 lakh loan changes the picture dramatically:

body.title: Regular EMI vs EMI plus ₹10,000 a month (₹80 lakh at 8%)

columns.label: Regular EMI of ₹66,915
points: More cash in hand each month

columns.label: EMI plus ₹10,000 (₹76,915)
points: Loan repaid in 178 months (14 years 10 months)

children.text: Leverage Over 10 Years: When the Loan Helps and When It Hurts

In Chapter 1 you saw leverage over a single year. Now let us run it over a full 10-year holding. Two investors buy identical ₹1 crore flats in Whitefield, Bengaluru, and sell after 10 years. Priya pays cash. Arjun puts down ₹20 lakh and borrows ₹80 lakh at 8% for 20 years. Both earn a 2.5% net rental yield, with rent rising 5% a year. The chart shows the annual return (IRR) each earns on their own money, under three price scenarios.

body.title: 10-year annual return on own money: cash vs loan (IRR, %, illustrative)
Show me the assumptions and cash flows

children.text: Flat price ₹1 crore; buying costs, maintenance changes and taxes are ignored to isolate the effect of the loan.
Net rent ₹2.5 lakh in year 1, growing 5% a year.
Arjun's EMIs: ₹66,915 × 12 = ₹8.03 lakh a year. In year 1, rent of ₹2.5 lakh minus EMIs of ₹8.03 lakh means he tops up about ₹5.53 lakh from his salary.
Sale after 10 years at 5% growth: ₹1 crore × 1.05^10 = ₹1.63 crore. Arjun repays the ₹55.15 lakh outstanding loan from the proceeds.
IRR is the single annual rate that makes all the money put in and taken out over the 10 years balance out. It is the fairest way to compare investments with uneven cash flows.

The results expose the rule. At 8% price growth, the flat earns roughly 10.5% a year in total, more than the 8% loan costs, so Arjun's return beats Priya's. At 5% growth, the flat earns about 7.5%, less than the loan's 8%, so borrowing actually lowers Arjun's return below Priya's, while he also tops up lakhs from his salary every year. At 2% growth, Arjun ends up with a negative return, and Priya still makes 4.84%.

body.latex: \text{Leverage helps only if} \quad \text{Net Rental Yield} + \text{Appreciation} > \text{Loan Interest Rate}
body.caption: Compare after-tax figures where possible. Tax deductions on loan interest can lower the effective loan cost; buying costs and tax on gains raise the hurdle.

body.title: Does the loan help?
body.question: A flat earns a 3% net rental yield and is expected to appreciate 4% a year. The home loan costs 8.5%. Ignoring tax, what effect is the loan likely to have on the investor's return on their own money?
options: Increase it, because leverage always magnifies returns
Reduce it, because the property's total return of about 7% is below the loan rate of 8.5%
No effect, because the loan is repaid over time
Increase it, because rent covers part of the EMI
body.explanation: Net yield plus appreciation is about 7%, less than the 8.5% loan rate. Every rupee borrowed costs more than it earns, so leverage drags the return on the investor's own money down, and magnifies losses if prices fall.

body.title: Tax benefits on home loans, in brief

content.caption: How home loan interest and principal are treated (simplified)

cells: Deductible up to ₹2 lakh a year
Within the ₹1.5 lakh overall limit for eligible investments and payments
Deductible against rent; loss set off against other income capped at ₹2 lakh, balance carried forward
Deductible against rent from that property; loss cannot be set off against other income

children.text: Tax benefits reduce the effective cost of a loan, but they rarely turn a bad property decision into a good one. Rules differ by regime and can change, so confirm the current position with a tax professional. Chapter 6 covers property taxation in more detail.

body.title: Ankit's first flat
body.scenario: Ankit, 28, earns ₹1.1 lakh a month take-home in Bengaluru and has ₹8 lakh saved. He wants a ₹75 lakh flat in Electronic City and asks the bank for a 90% loan over 25 years because "the EMI is lower." He plans to rent it out, since his office moves to Whitefield next year.
body.prompt: What problems will Ankit run into, and how should he rethink the plan?
body.modelAnswer:
1. LTV cap: a loan above ₹30 lakh is capped at 80% LTV. On ₹75 lakh, the maximum loan is ₹60 lakh, so he needs ₹15 lakh down, not ₹7.5 lakh.
2. Cash shortfall: on top of the ₹15 lakh down payment, Karnataka stamp duty, registration and other charges could add roughly ₹6 lakh or more. His ₹8 lakh savings is far short, and banks will not fund these charges.
3. Tenure trade-off: a ₹60 lakh loan at 8% costs about ₹46,309 a month over 25 years vs ₹50,186 over 20 years. The longer tenure saves ₹3,877 a month but adds about ₹18.5 lakh in total interest.
4. Affordability: an EMI of ₹46,000 to ₹50,000 is about 42% to 46% of his take-home pay, at the edge of what lenders allow, with no buffer for emergencies or rate rises.
5. Leverage maths: Electronic City rent might give a 3% to 4% gross yield, well below an 8% loan rate. Unless prices rise strongly, borrowing reduces his return, and he will top up the EMI from salary every month.
6. Rethink: build savings for a proper down payment plus charges and an emergency fund, consider a smaller or cheaper flat, or rent near the new Whitefield office and invest through REITs or index funds until the numbers work.

body.title: Before You Sign a Home Loan
steps: Calculate total interest over the full tenure, not just the EMI
Check the LTV cap for your loan size and fund the down payment plus all charges from savings
Keep total EMIs comfortably below 40% of take-home pay, with an emergency fund of at least 6 months
Compare the property's net yield plus realistic appreciation against the loan rate
Ask how the lender handles rate changes: EMI increase or tenure extension
Plan regular prepayments, which carry no charges on floating-rate loans for individuals under current RBI rules
Check which tax regime you are in before counting on any deduction

cards.definition: Equated Monthly Instalment: a fixed payment covering interest and principal that repays the loan over its tenure.
The gradual repayment of a loan, with early EMIs mostly interest and later EMIs mostly principal.
Loan as a percentage of property value. RBI caps it at 90%, 80% or 75% depending on loan size.
The rate at which the RBI lends to banks; most floating home loan rates are linked to it.
Keeping the EMI unchanged after a rate rise by adding months to the loan, which sharply increases total interest.
Paying extra principal ahead of schedule to cut interest and tenure.
Internal Rate of Return: the single annual rate that balances all money invested and received over time.

points: An ₹80 lakh loan at 8% for 20 years costs ₹66,915 a month and ₹80.6 lakh in interest, more than the loan itself.
Early EMIs are mostly interest: after 10 years of EMIs on that loan, ₹55.15 lakh is still owed.
RBI caps home loans at 90%, 80% or 75% of property value depending on loan size, and banks generally do not fund stamp duty or other charges.
Floating rates follow the repo rate; letting a lender extend tenure after a rate rise can add years and lakhs of interest.
Prepaying even ₹10,000 a month can save over ₹23 lakh of interest, and floating-rate home loans for individuals carry no prepayment charges under current RBI rules.
Leverage raises returns only when net yield plus appreciation exceeds the loan rate; otherwise it lowers returns and magnifies losses.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not financial, tax or investment advice. Loan rates, lender policies and tax rules vary and change over time, and the return scenarios use simplified, illustrative assumptions. Consult your lender, a tax professional and a SEBI-registered investment adviser before borrowing to buy property.
